lead: This unit is about first-order partial differential equations: how they are formed, sorted and solved. You learn the four standard nonlinear types, Lagrange's linear equation, Charpit's method, the Cauchy problem, and the advanced Pfaffian equation.
about: The unit starts with 4.1, where differentiating a relation and removing arbitrary constants or functions produces a first-order PDE. Chapter 4.2 sorts nonlinear PDEs into four standard types and reduces each to an ODE. Chapter 4.3 handles the linear form Pp+Qq=R through its auxiliary system. Chapter 4.4 gives Charpit's general method for equations outside those types. Chapter 4.5 adds an initial curve and asks for the unique integral surface—the Cauchy problem. Chapter 4.6, taught by only a few universities, treats Pfaffian equations Pdx+Qdy+Rdz=0 and their integrability condition. Each chapter supplies the p, q and integration tools the next one uses, ending with a complete first-order toolkit.

chapters.idea: A PDE is born when you differentiate a relation enough times and remove the arbitrary constants or functions.
chapters.depth: Define p = ∂z/∂x and q = ∂z/∂y first. For arbitrary constants: differentiate the relation with respect to x and y, then eliminate the constants. Two constants give a first-order PDE; one constant may also give first order. For arbitrary functions: if z = f(u), use p u_y − q u_x = 0; if f(u,v)=0, use the Jacobian u_x v_y − u_y v_x = 0. Some syllabi call this 'formation of PDE' or 'elimination of arbitrary constants and functions'. Do not drift into solving.

figure.title: Forming a PDE from z = ax + by + ab
figure.aria: Flowchart shows differentiating z = ax + by + ab to get p = a and q = b, then substituting to form z = px + qy + pq.

chapters.example: Form the PDE by eliminating the arbitrary constants a and b from z = ax + by + ab. Worked: p = a and q = b, so z = px + qy + pq.
chapters.trap: Do not differentiate z as if a and b were variables. Also two arbitrary functions usually give a second-order PDE, not a first-order one.
chapters.prereq: Partial differentiation from first-year calculus; p and q are defined here.
chapters.leave: Solving the formed PDE to 4.2–4.4; second-order formation to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Four standard shapes of first-order nonlinear PDEs each reduce to an ODE by a fixed substitution.
chapters.depth: Cover the four standard types and their fixed substitutions: (1) f(p,q)=0: z=ax+by+c with f(a,b)=0. (2) f(z,p,q)=0: u=x+ay, p=dz/du, q=a dz/du, solve the ODE. (3) f(x,p,q)=0: set q=a, solve p=φ(x,a), integrate dz=p dx+a dy. (4) f(y,p,q)=0: set p=a, solve q=ψ(y,a), integrate dz=a dx+q dy. Mention Clairaut's form z=px+qy+f(p,q) as an extension. Some syllabi add variable separable: try z=X(x)Y(y) for linear PDEs. Some exclude equations reducible to standard types; keep those out.

figure.aria: Tree sorts a first-order PDE into the four standard types, with the substitution for each type.

chapters.example: Solve p² + q² = 1. Worked: this is f(p,q)=0. Let p=a and q=b with a²+b²=1, so b=√(1−a²). The complete integral is z = ax + √(1−a²) y + c, with a an arbitrary constant and |a|≤1.
chapters.trap: Do not use q=a in f(z,p,q)=0; there the substitution is u=x+ay. In f(y,p,q)=0 set p=a, not q=a. A complete integral is a family, not the unique solution.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for p and q; Unit 1 for solving the reduced ODE.
chapters.leave: General nonlinear equations to 4.4; linear equations to 4.3; second-order separation to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A linear first-order PDE Pp+Qq=R is solved by two independent integrals of its auxiliary system.
chapters.depth: Lagrange's linear equation P p + Q q = R with P,Q,R functions of x,y,z. Write auxiliary equations dx/P=dy/Q=dz/R. Two independent integrals u=c₁, v=c₂ give φ(u,v)=0 or u=f(v). Use multipliers to find integrals. Geometrical meaning: each solution is an integral surface. Some syllabi call it 'Lagrange's linear PDE' or 'linear equation of first order'. Keep to linear; Charpit is for nonlinear.

figure.title: Lagrange example (y−z)p+(z−x)q=x−y
figure.aria: Flowchart shows the auxiliary ratios for the example and two multiplier choices that yield x+y+z=c₁ and x²+y²+z²=c₂.

chapters.example: Solve (y − z)p + (z − x)q = x − y. Worked: auxiliary equations are dx/(y−z)=dy/(z−x)=dz/(x−y). Multipliers 1,1,1 give x+y+z=c₁. Multipliers x,y,z give x²+y²+z²=c₂. The general solution is φ(x+y+z, x²+y²+z²)=0.
chapters.trap: The denominators are P,Q,R, not p,q,r; and two first integrals must be independent. Do not force z as the subject unless asked.
chapters.prereq: 4.1 for p,q; integration of exact differentials.
chapters.leave: Nonlinear equations to 4.4; Pfaffian equations to 4.6; second-order linear PDEs to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Charpit builds a second relation between p and q, then integrates dz=p dx+q dy to get a complete integral.
chapters.depth: General first-order PDE F(x,y,z,p,q)=0. Write Charpit's auxiliary equations dx/F_p = dy/F_q = dz/(pF_p+qF_q) = −dp/(F_x+pF_z) = −dq/(F_y+qF_z). Find one integral f(x,y,z,p,q,a)=0, solve it with F for p and q, then integrate dz=p dx+q dy. Use for nonlinear equations outside 4.2 and for Clairaut if asked. Mention the Lagrange special case but do not re-teach 4.3.

figure.title: Charpit's method
figure.aria: Flowchart shows Charpit's auxiliary equations giving one integral, then p and q, then integration of dz to a complete integral.

chapters.example: Solve p q = z by Charpit's method. Worked: F=pq−z=0. Charpit gives dx/q = dy/p = dz/(2pq) = dp/p = dq/q. From dp/p=dq/q, p=a q. Substitute: a q²=z, so q=√(z/a) and p=√(a z). Then dz = √(z/a)(a dx + dy). Integrate: 2√z = (a x + y + b)/√a. Square: 4a z = (a x + y + b)².
chapters.trap: Losing the minus signs in −dp and −dq is the common error. After finding p and q, integrate dz=p dx+q dy only after substituting them in terms of x,y,z.
chapters.leave: Initial data selection to 4.5; Pfaffian form to 4.6.

chapters.idea: The Cauchy problem asks for the one integral surface of a first-order PDE that contains a given initial curve.
chapters.depth: Define the Cauchy problem: F(x,y,z,p,q)=0 plus initial curve x=x₀(s), y=y₀(s), z=z₀(s). Add p₀,q₀ satisfying F=0 and the strip condition dz₀/ds = p₀ dx₀/ds + q₀ dy₀/ds. Solve characteristic ODEs from the initial curve; if the curve is not characteristic, a unique integral surface exists locally. Some syllabi call it Cauchy's method of characteristics. If your syllabus adds numerical method of lines with RK4, give one short extension: discretize y, solve ODEs in x with RK4.

figure.title: Cauchy problem for a first-order PDE
figure.aria: Flowchart shows initial curve and strip condition feeding characteristic equations, with a non-characteristic check before the unique surface.

chapters.example: Solve p + q = 1 with z = 0 on the line x + y = 0. Worked: the general solution is z = x + f(x−y). On x+y=0, y=−x, so 0 = x + f(2x). Hence f(u) = −u/2. Therefore z = x − (x−y)/2 = (x+y)/2. Check: p=q=1/2, so p+q=1, and z=0 when x+y=0.
chapters.trap: An initial curve must satisfy the strip condition; otherwise the data is inconsistent. A characteristic initial curve may give no unique surface.
chapters.prereq: 4.4 for characteristic equations; Unit 1 for initial value ideas.
chapters.leave: Second-order Cauchy problems such as the wave equation to Unit 5; numerical method of lines to a numerical methods course or a short extension.

chapters.idea: A Pfaffian equation P dx+Q dy+R dz=0 is integrable only when a certain curl condition holds; then it gives a family of surfaces.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Pfaffian Pdx+Qdy+Rdz=0. Integrability condition: P(∂R/∂y−∂Q/∂z)+Q(∂P/∂z−∂R/∂x)+R(∂Q/∂x−∂P/∂y)=0. Exactness is stronger: P=∂u/∂x, Q=∂u/∂y, R=∂u/∂z. Solve by inspection, multipliers, or as an ODE. Geometrical meaning: solution surfaces u=c are orthogonal to the curves dx/P=dy/Q=dz/R, because (P,Q,R)·(dx,dy,dz)=0.

figure.title: Pfaffian equation and integrability

nodes.label: Pfaffian
nodes.note: P dx + Q dy + R dz = 0

figure.aria: Flowchart shows the integrability test for a Pfaffian equation, the stronger exactness check, and the surface orthogonal to the curves dx/P=dy/Q=dz/R.

chapters.example: Solve yz dx + zx dy + xy dz = 0. Worked: notice d(xyz)=yz dx+xz dy+xy dz, so xyz=c. Check exactness: ∂(yz)/∂y=z=∂(zx)/∂x, ∂(zx)/∂z=x=∂(xy)/∂y, ∂(xy)/∂x=y=∂(yz)/∂z.
chapters.trap: The integrability condition is not the same as exactness. A Pfaffian can be integrable with an integrating factor but not exact. Also do not call every Pdx+Qdy+Rdz=0 exact—check the stronger equalities.
chapters.prereq: 4.3 for dx/P=dy/Q=dz/R; exact differentials from Unit 1.
chapters.leave: General first-order solution methods to 4.2–4.5; second-order surfaces to Unit 5.
